clue.text: Part of Manhattan is sedate surprisingly

indicators.note: surprisingly hints that the letters of 'is sedate' end up in an unexpected new order

explanation.surface: A remark that a New York district is unexpectedly calm.
explanation.definitionFit: The East Side is the eastern district of the island of Manhattan in New York City.

clue.text: Difficult situation in Stoke Poges churchyard, reportedly?

indicators.note: reportedly means we hear the phrase rather than see it, so the spelling may change

parts.note: Thomas Gray wrote his Elegy in the churchyard at Stoke Poges

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about some trouble in a famous English village churchyard.
explanation.walkthrough: Stoke Poges is a Buckinghamshire village whose churchyard inspired Thomas Gray's Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard; GRAY AREA said aloud is GREY AREA.
explanation.definitionFit: A grey area is an ambiguous matter with no clear rule, which makes for a tricky situation.

clue.text: Not a sort of dreamy movement set up in Oxford college

indicators.note: in a down clue, set up means the letters are raised, read from bottom to top

parts.note: taken as the word itself
REM is rapid eye movement, the sleep phase when we dream

explanation.surface: Something about a dreamlike motion staged at an Oxford college.
explanation.definitionFit: Merton is one of the oldest colleges of the University of Oxford.

clue.text: PM to resign? Has to go about it tortuously

indicators.note: to go about means to surround, so the rearranged letters sit round the other piece
tortuously, twisting this way and that, says the letters of 'Has' are jumbled

parts.note: to resign is to quit

explanation.surface: A prime minister considers stepping down and must find a winding route to do so.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it' refers back to 'to resign': ASH, the jumbled HAS, goes about QUIT.
explanation.definitionFit: H. H. Asquith was the Liberal Prime Minister of Britain from 1908 to 1916.

clue.text: Rest in sweet place with ruined houses?

indicators.note: in places the resting word inside the dessert word

parts.note: a bombe is a frozen dome-shaped dessert, a sweet
to rest is to sit

explanation.surface: An invitation to relax in a pleasant spot that has wrecked buildings.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain 'sweet' commonly means a dessert course.
explanation.definitionFit: A bomb site is an area where buildings were destroyed by bombing, as in wartime London.

clue.text: Looking to keep home that houses nothing innovative

indicators.note: to keep means the looking word holds the rest inside it

parts.note: looking closely is peering

indicators.note: houses means contains, so the home word holds the nothing

parts.note: at home is in, so home gives IN
nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: Someone seeking a house with nothing inside is being original.
explanation.definitionFit: Pioneering work breaks new ground, being the first of its kind.

clue.text: Worship has some here very uplifted

indicators.note: in a down clue, uplifted means the letters are read from bottom to top
some says only part of the following words is taken

parts.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: A remark that worship here leaves people greatly raised in spirit.
explanation.definitionFit: To revere is to hold in deep respect or adore, as one worships.

clue.text: What Jacob was? Leader of House — stuffy with it

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter

parts.note: a stuffy room is airless

explanation.surface: A political jibe about Jacob as Leader of the House, a stuffy figure.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface evokes Jacob Rees-Mogg, Leader of the House of Commons; the biblical Jacob was smooth-skinned, unlike his hairy brother Esau.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis Jacob says 'my brother Esau is a hairy man, and I am a smooth man'.

clue.text: Sadly, I'm doubter about one court making a passing comment

indicators.note: about means around, so the rearranged letters surround the rest
sadly signals the letters of 'I'm doubter' are put into a sorry, disordered state

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A sceptic regretfully comments on a court in passing.
explanation.definitionFit: An obiter dictum is a judge's incidental remark, Latin for something said by the way.

clue.text: Don't visit state flooded by river — awash with wood destroyed

indicators.note: the state word is flooded, filled up, by what follows

parts.note: to state is to say
the Tay is the longest river in Scotland

indicators.note: the wood is destroyed, removed from the word awash

parts.note: taken as the word itself
ash is a tree and its timber

explanation.surface: A flood warning: keep out of a region swamped by a river, its forests wrecked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Awash' fits the flood picture, but here it is just letters to be cut down. The Tay is a Scottish river.
explanation.definitionFit: To stay away from somewhere is to keep clear of it and not go there.

clue.text: Reading material with digital access

parts.note: sounds like an e-book, but 'digital' means of the fingers: notches you put a thumb in to open a book

explanation.walkthrough: 'Digital' suggests computers; here it means using a digit, a finger or thumb.
explanation.definitionFit: A reference book's edge has cut tabs, one per letter, letting a thumb flip straight to a section.

clue.text: See 22 down
Repairs past being done when one is lacking ___ ?

definitions.text: Repairs past being done when one is lacking ___ ?

indicators.note: done here means processed or worked over, so the letters are rearranged
lacking means the named letter must be removed from the fodder

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: Repairs can't be finished when the necessary components are missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove I from REPAIRS PAST and rearrange; the whole clue also describes the answer, the blank standing for it.
explanation.definitionFit: Spare parts are replacement components; without them a mechanic cannot complete a repair.

clue.text: Attempts to cross French sea, being back in boats

indicators.note: to cross here means to span the other piece, which sits within

parts.note: attempts are tries

indicators.note: being back means the letters are read in reverse

parts.note: mer is French for sea

explanation.surface: Efforts to sail across a French sea, returning in vessels.
explanation.definitionFit: Triremes were ancient Greek and Roman warships rowed with three banks of oars.

clue.text: End of road — politician in criminal case bunks off

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter
in puts the politician inside the rearranged letters
criminal suggests something crooked, so the letters of case are twisted

parts.note: MP is Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A politician implicated in a crime makes a run for it at the road's end.
explanation.walkthrough: To bunk off is British slang for slipping away or playing truant.
explanation.definitionFit: To decamp is to depart suddenly or secretly, which is what one does in bunking off.

clue.text: Travellers gloomy, drinking beer? Quite the opposite

indicators.note: drinking means taking in, so one word goes inside the other
says the containment runs the other way: the beer takes in the gloomy word

parts.note: Pils is a pale lager, short for Pilsner
gloomy means grim

explanation.surface: Downcast wayfarers have a drink, or rather the reverse.
explanation.definitionFit: Pilgrims are people journeying, often to a holy site, so they are travellers.

clue.text: We turned up to be enthralled by dog showing charm

indicators.note: enthralled by means held captive inside the dog word

parts.note: a bitch is a female dog

indicators.note: turned up here means turned over, so the letters run backwards

explanation.surface: We arrived to be captivated by a dog with a winning manner.
explanation.definitionFit: To bewitch is to cast a spell over, to enchant or charm.

clue.text: Upper-class lady against benefit being raised

parts.note: con means against, as in pros and cons

indicators.note: in a down clue, raised means the letters read upwards, in reverse

parts.note: an asset is a benefit or advantage

explanation.surface: A posh woman objects to her allowance going up.
explanation.definitionFit: A contessa is an Italian countess, a woman of noble rank.

clue.text: Criminal receiver getting hold of excellent ceramic ware

indicators.note: getting hold of means grasping the other piece within

parts.note: a fence deals in stolen goods
A1 means first-rate, written AI

explanation.surface: A dealer in stolen goods acquires some fine pottery.
explanation.definitionFit: Faience is tin-glazed earthenware pottery, named after Faenza in Italy.

clue.text: All mice out to eat a shrub

indicators.note: to eat means to take something inside, so the rearranged letters hold the extra one
out, as in put out of order, says the letters of 'All mice' are rearranged

explanation.surface: Every mouse comes out to nibble a bush.
explanation.definitionFit: The camellia is an evergreen flowering bush related to the tea plant.

clue.text: Depression associated with member facing endless shame

indicators.note: facing places the limb word in front of the next piece

parts.note: an arm is a member, a limb

indicators.note: endless means the final letter is dropped

parts.note: 'what a shame' means 'what a pity'

explanation.surface: Low spirits tied to a club member confronting unending disgrace.
explanation.definitionFit: The armpit is the hollow under the shoulder, a depression in the body.

clue.text: Some pang in animals? Certainly in humans!

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Asks whether beasts feel chest pains, then insists people certainly do.
explanation.definitionFit: Angina is chest pain from reduced blood flow to the heart, a familiar human condition.

clue.text: A hostile bang smashed by champion tennis player

indicators.note: smashed means broken up, so the letters are rearranged; also a tennis stroke

explanation.surface: An aggressive shot is smashed away by a tennis champion.
explanation.definitionFit: Althea Gibson was the first Black player to win Wimbledon and US titles, in 1957 and 1958.

clue.text: Troublemaker on broadcast intended being heartless, creating harm

parts.note: an imp is a mischievous troublemaker
to air is to broadcast

indicators.note: heartless means the middle letter is removed

parts.note: intended means meant

explanation.surface: A mischief-maker on the radio deliberately cruel, doing damage.
explanation.definitionFit: Impairment is damage or weakening, a lessening of function, which is harm.

clue.text: See 2
See 10
See 9
Crack from cleric, idiot in church

indicators.note: in puts the cleric and idiot inside the church letters

parts.note: CE is the Church of England
Rev is short for Reverend, a cleric
an ass is a fool

explanation.surface: An insult hurled by a vicar at a fool in church.
explanation.definitionFit: A crevasse is a deep crack or fissure, especially in a glacier.
